# Abstract

## Structured abstract

Background

Cardiovascular diseases (CVDs) remain the leading cause of death worldwide, yet most of this burden is attributable to modifiable risk factors. The WHO has endorsed ambitious targets for hypertension control and lipid-lowering therapy coverage by 2030, but the long-term health gains achievable across the full spectrum of country income levels have not been quantified.

Methods

We used a discrete-time multi-state transition model (Well, Sick, Dead) calibrated to Global Burden of Disease 2023 epidemiological data and United Nations World Population Prospects 2024 demographic projections. The model was applied to `r n_countries` countries over the period `r study_years`, projecting mortality from four CVD causes: ischaemic heart disease, ischaemic stroke, intracerebral haemorrhage, and hypertensive heart disease. Three intervention scenarios --- hypertension control in the general population (50% control by 2030), hypertension control among people with diabetes (80% control by 2030), and lipid-lowering therapy scale-up (50% coverage by 2030) --- were modelled individually and in combination against a business-as-usual reference scenario.

Findings

Simultaneous achievement of all three WHO targets was projected to avert `r fmt_m(total_all)` million CVD deaths over `r study_years`, representing `r pct_all`% of business-as-usual CVD mortality. Hypertension control in the general population contributed the largest single-intervention effect (`r fmt_m(total_bp)` million deaths averted; `r pct_bp`%), followed by lipid-lowering therapy (`r fmt_m(total_stat)` million; `r pct_stat`%) and targeted blood pressure control in people with diabetes (`r fmt_m(total_bpd)` million; `r pct_bpd`%). Ischaemic heart disease accounted for the largest share of avertable deaths. Benefits accrued predominantly in adults aged 70 years and older and were concentrated in countries with the highest baseline CVD burden.

Interpretation

Achieving WHO cardiovascular risk-factor targets by 2030 could avert millions of CVD deaths over the subsequent 25 years across `r n_countries` countries. These findings provide a quantitative foundation for national and global investment in hypertension management and lipid-lowering therapy scale-up as complementary strategies for CVD prevention.

## Research in context

Evidence before this study

Previous modelling studies have demonstrated the effectiveness of blood pressure lowering and statin therapy for reducing cardiovascular events at the individual and single-country levels. The NCD Countdown collaborations have tracked progress toward SDG target 3.4 and identified efficient intervention packages for low- and middle-income countries [@Bennett2020NCD2030Path; @Watkins2022NCD2030]. However, prior global analyses have typically been limited to single interventions, short projection horizons, or restricted country coverage, making it difficult to quantify the combined, long-term health returns of achieving multiple WHO cardiovascular targets simultaneously across the full range of country settings.

Added value of this study

This study provides the first comprehensive global projection of CVD deaths avertable from simultaneous achievement of WHO targets for hypertension control and lipid-lowering therapy across `r n_countries` countries over a 25-year horizon. By modelling country-specific epidemiological and demographic trajectories and applying intervention effects based on meta-analytic evidence, it quantifies the magnitude, timing, and distribution of health gains by cause, age, sex, WHO region, and World Bank income group.

Implications of all the available evidence

The evidence supports prioritising concurrent investment in hypertension management and lipid-lowering therapy as complementary, high-impact strategies for reducing global CVD mortality. The benefits are largest in absolute terms in high-burden countries, but proportional gains are substantial across all income groups, reinforcing the case for universal scale-up through primary health care platforms such as the WHO HEARTS technical package.

# Introduction
Cardiovascular diseases (CVDs) remain the world's leading cause of death and disability-adjusted life years (DALYs). CVD deaths increased globally from 13.1 million in 1990 to 19.2 million in 2023, with ischaemic heart disease, intracerebral haemorrhagic stroke, ischaemic stroke, and hypertensive heart disease among the leading causes [@Chong2024]. Age-standardized CVD DALY rates were highest in low and low-middle Socio-demographic Index (SDI) settings, and the number of prevalent CVD cases more than doubled between 1990 and 2023, rising from 311 million to 626 million. In 2023, modifiable risk factors accounted for 79.6% of CVD burden, equivalent to 347 million DALYs --- underscoring that the majority of this burden is preventable.

Among modifiable exposures, high systolic blood pressure and high low-density lipoprotein (LDL) cholesterol rank as the two leading contributors to attributable CVD burden worldwide, together accounting for a greater share of ischaemic heart disease and stroke mortality than dietary risks, air pollution, or any other single risk factor [@Vollset2024]. The scale of unmet need is striking: 1.4 billion adults live with high blood pressure, yet only 23% have it under control [@Banigbe2025]. The estimated global prevalence of hypercholesterolaemia was 24.1% in 2025, and that of hypertriglyceridaemia 28.8%, with statin therapy coverage remaining far below levels needed for meaningful population-level risk reduction [@Basios2025]. Beyond their magnitude of effect, blood pressure control and lipid-lowering therapy are distinguished by the availability of effective, affordable, and scalable pharmaceutical interventions and established primary health care delivery platforms --- making them implementation priorities of the highest order [@Moran2024].

Multiple multilateral frameworks now reflect convergent political commitment to tackling these two risk factors as a cornerstone of NCD prevention. WHO Member States have endorsed progressively ambitious targets: the 2021 Global Diabetes Compact committed to 80% blood pressure control and systematic statin therapy for all adults aged 40 years and above with diabetes. The WHO NCD Global Monitoring Framework set a target of at least 50% of eligible high-risk individuals receiving effective drug therapies, including statins, by 2025; and the Political Declaration of the Fourth High-level Meeting on NCDs (2025) called for 80% of primary health care facilities to stock WHO-recommended essential medicines by 2030, alongside control of blood pressure in an additional 150 million people. The present study quantifies what achieving these targets would mean in practice --- in health and economic terms, across `r n_countries` countries.

Although the clinical benefits of these interventions are well established, comparable global evidence quantifying the long-term mortality, morbidity, and economic returns of simultaneously achieving both targets across the full spectrum of country income levels remains limited. Existing analyses have typically been restricted to single countries, short time horizons, or individual interventions modelled in isolation [@Kontis2019; @Pickersgill2022], constraining the ability of national governments, international donors, and health institutions to prioritise investment and plan implementation at scale.

This study addresses that gap by estimating the health outcomes associated with achieving WHO targets for hypertension control and lipid-lowering therapy across `r n_countries` countries from 2026 to 2050, using a comparative risk assessment modelling framework applied to country-specific epidemiological and demographic data.

# Methods

## Study design

We conducted a multi-country comparative modelling study using a discrete-time multi-state transition model projecting CVD mortality across `r n_countries` countries from 2026 to 2050. Four causes of CVD death were modelled jointly: ischaemic heart disease (IHD), ischaemic stroke, intracerebral haemorrhage (haemorrhagic stroke), and hypertensive heart disease. Three health states --- Well, Sick, and Dead --- were tracked for each cause, stratified by single year of age (20--95), sex, and country. The model was calibrated to observed epidemiological data from 2019 and projected forward using annual time steps (see Multi-State Transition Model).

## Data sources

Death counts and mortality rates were derived from the World Health Organization Global Health Estimates (GHE). Prevalence estimates were obtained from the Global Burden of Disease (GBD) 2023 study. Population denominators were taken from the United Nations World Population Prospects 2024 revision, using single-year age- and sex-specific projections for each country. Blood pressure distributions were sourced from the NCD Risk Factor Collaboration, and baseline hypertension control rates were based on country-level analyses provided by WHO. Relative risks for blood pressure reduction were based on the meta-analysis by Ettehad et al. [-@Ettehad2016], stratified by blood pressure category and cause. COVID-19 excess mortality was applied for 2020--2021 only. Statin coverage estimates were derived from published and imputed country-level data, with intervention effect sizes drawn from established randomised controlled trial evidence [@Fulcher2015].


## Intervention scenarios

Three active intervention scenarios were modelled against a business-as-usual (BAU) reference in which 2024 coverage rates were held constant through 2050:

1. **Hypertension control (general population):** Linear scale-up of population-level blood pressure control by 2030, beginning in 2026, corresponding to the WHO target of 150 million additional people with controlled hypertension. Effect sizes were derived from the Ettehad et al. meta-analysis, applied across eight blood pressure bins with incremental coverage above baseline generating new risk reductions for incidence and case fatality (see Hypertension Control Intervention Model).

2. **Hypertension control (diabetes subgroup):** Linear scale-up to 80% blood pressure control among people with diagnosed diabetes by 2030. Effect sizes were weighted by country-level diabetes prevalence and blended with general-population hypertension effects (see Hypertension Control Intervention Model: Diabetes Component).

3. **Lipid-lowering therapy:** Linear scale-up to 50% statin coverage among eligible adults (aged 40 years and older) by 2030. Effects were restricted to IHD and ischaemic stroke and applied through an attributable-fraction approach, with an atherosclerotic fraction of 0.60 for ischaemic stroke (see Statin Therapy Intervention Model).

A fourth combination scenario applied all three interventions simultaneously, with effects combining multiplicatively across interventions (see Multi-State Transition Model).

## Modelling framework

The core model is a discrete-time state-transition framework in which individuals move between Well, Sick, and Dead states at each annual time step according to cause-specific incidence rates (Well to Sick), case fatality rates (Sick to Dead), and background mortality rates (all states to Dead). Interventions modify incidence and case fatality through multiplicative effect ratios ($\varepsilon_{IR}$, $\varepsilon_{CF}$), which are computed from the intervention-specific coverage increment above baseline. Only incremental coverage above baseline was credited with new effects, avoiding double-counting of existing treatment benefits. For hypertension control, effect ratios are derived from a nine-step pipeline incorporating blood pressure bin distributions, GBD relative risks, Ettehad trial effect sizes, and population-weighted aggregation. For statin therapy, incremental coverage generates cause- and location-specific risk reductions applied to incidence and case fatality. Under the combined scenario, effects combine multiplicatively: $\varepsilon_{IR,\text{total}} = \varepsilon_{IR,\text{BP}} \times \varepsilon_{IR,\text{statin}}$ (see Mathematical Notation Summary).

## Calibration

Incidence (IR) and case fatality (CF) parameters were calibrated jointly to ensure consistency with external data sources: incidence rates were adjusted to reproduce age-, sex-, country-, and cause-specific incidence patterns from GBD 2023, while case-fatality parameters were calibrated to match observed cause-specific mortality counts from WHO GHE within each stratum. COVID-19 excess mortality was incorporated for 2020–2021 only (see Key Parameter Appendix).


## Data and code availability

All input data used in this analysis are publicly available from their original sources (e.g., WHO Global Health Estimates). Processed inputs and model code are provided in the project repository: https://github.com/Disease-Control-Priorities/uw-who-cvdtargets. Model outputs (results) can be accessed and downloaded at the same link. All analyses were conducted in R (version 4.5.1), and full scripts are openly available in the repository.


## Outcomes

The primary outcome was cumulative CVD deaths averted relative to the BAU scenario over 2026--2050, disaggregated by intervention, cause of death, age group, sex, WHO region, and World Bank income group. Secondary outcomes included years of life lost (YLLs) averted, years lived with disability (YLDs) averted, disability-adjusted life years (DALYs) averted, and age-standardised mortality rates (ASMR) over time.

Burden of disease was quantified using three complementary metrics: years of life lost (YLL), years lived with disability (YLD), and disability-adjusted life years (DALY), where $DALY = YLL + YLD$. Remaining life expectancy at each age of death was obtained from the United Nations World Population Prospects 2024 revision (medium variant), providing country- and year-specific values. Disability weights were derived from GBD 2023 data as the ratio of cause-specific YLDs to prevalence for each cause and location. No age weighting or time discounting was applied; all estimates are undiscounted (see Supplemental Material: DALY Calculation Methods).

## Sensitivity and uncertainty analysis

The model was run under the primary set of assumptions described above. Formal probabilistic sensitivity analysis incorporating GBD uncertainty intervals and parameter distributions is planned as a subsequent extension. The present analysis reports central estimates derived from mean input parameters.

# Results

## Baseline global trajectory, 2026--2050

Under the business-as-usual scenario, in which hypertension control and statin coverage remained at 2024 levels, the model projected `r fmt_m(bau_total_deaths)` million cumulative CVD deaths from all four causes across `r n_countries` countries over 2026--2050 (Supplemental Figure \@ref(fig:fig1-paper)). Ischaemic heart disease was the dominant contributor, followed by ischaemic stroke, intracerebral haemorrhage, and hypertensive heart disease. Global incident and prevalent CVD cases continued to rise over the projection period, driven by population ageing. Age-standardised CVD mortality rates declined modestly even under the BAU scenario, reflecting projected demographic transitions, but absolute death counts increased as population growth outpaced age-specific rate reductions.

## Global impact of achieving the hypertension control target

Achievement of the WHO target for hypertension control in the general population (50% control by 2030) was projected to avert `r fmt_m(total_bp)` million CVD deaths over `r study_years`, equivalent to `r pct_bp`% of BAU mortality (Table 1; Supplemental Figure \@ref(fig:fig2-paper)). The annual number of deaths averted grew steadily from the onset of scale-up in 2026, reaching `r fmt_k(annual_2030_bp)` thousand per year by 2030 and `r fmt_k(annual_2050_bp)` thousand per year by 2050, as the cumulative exposure to lower blood pressure compounded over time (Supplemental Figure \@ref(fig:fig3-paper)). The benefits of hypertension control spanned all four CVD causes, with ischaemic heart disease and ischaemic stroke accounting for the majority of averted deaths, followed by intracerebral haemorrhage and hypertensive heart disease (Table 2). In terms of disease burden, hypertension control in the general population was projected to avert `r fmt_m(total_dalys_bp)` million DALYs over the study period.

Targeted hypertension control among people with diabetes (80% control by 2030) was projected to avert an additional `r fmt_m(total_bpd)` million deaths (`r pct_bpd`% of BAU) and `r fmt_m(total_dalys_bpd)` million DALYs, reflecting the elevated cardiovascular risk in this subgroup and the higher coverage target.

## Global impact of achieving the lipid-lowering therapy target

Scale-up of lipid-lowering therapy to 50% coverage among eligible adults by 2030 was projected to avert `r fmt_m(total_stat)` million deaths over `r study_years` (`r pct_stat`% of BAU; Table 1). Because statin effects were restricted to ischaemic heart disease and ischaemic stroke, the cause-specific profile of averted deaths differed from the hypertension scenarios: ischaemic heart disease accounted for `r fmt_m(averted_ihd_stat)` million averted deaths and ischaemic stroke for `r fmt_m(averted_istroke_stat)` million (Table 2). The annual trajectory of benefit was similar in shape to that of hypertension control, with gains accelerating after 2030 as sustained coverage translated into cumulative risk reduction (Supplemental Figure \@ref(fig:fig3-paper)). Lipid-lowering therapy was projected to avert `r fmt_m(total_dalys_stat)` million DALYs over the study period.

## Combined impact of both targets

Simultaneous achievement of all three WHO targets was projected to avert `r fmt_m(total_all)` million CVD deaths over `r study_years`, representing `r pct_all`% of cumulative BAU mortality (Table 1; Supplemental Figure \@ref(fig:fig2-paper)). The combined scenario yielded substantially greater benefits than any single intervention alone, because hypertension control and statin therapy act on partially overlapping but distinct causal pathways and their effects combined multiplicatively. By 2050, the all-interventions scenario was averting approximately `r fmt_k(annual_2050_all)` thousand deaths annually relative to BAU (Figure \@ref(fig:fig4-paper)). The combined scenario was projected to avert `r fmt_m(total_dalys_all)` million DALYs, `r fmt_m(total_ylls_all)` million YLLs, and `r fmt_m(total_ylds_all)` million YLDs over the study period (Table 3).

Ischaemic heart disease was the leading cause of averted deaths under the combined scenario (`r fmt_m(averted_ihd_all)` million), followed by ischaemic stroke (`r fmt_m(averted_istroke_all)` million), intracerebral haemorrhage (`r fmt_m(averted_hstroke_all)` million), and hypertensive heart disease (`r fmt_m(averted_hhd_all)` million; Table 2).

## Heterogeneity across regions and income groups

The distribution of projected health gains was heterogeneous across WHO regions. Regional totals reflected the combination of population size, baseline CVD burden, and current coverage gaps, with regions characterised by high hypertension prevalence and low baseline treatment rates exhibiting the largest proportional reductions (Table 4).

When stratified by World Bank income group, low-income and lower-middle-income countries together accounted for a substantial share of avertable deaths and DALYs, underscoring the equity implications of global target achievement (Table 5). Upper-middle-income countries, which include several of the world's most populous nations, contributed the largest absolute volumes of averted burden. High-income countries showed smaller proportional gains, consistent with their higher baseline treatment coverage.

## Distribution by age and sex

The projected benefits of all interventions were concentrated among older adults. Under the combined scenario, adults aged 70 years and older accounted for `r fmt_m(averted_70_79 + averted_80_89 + averted_90p)` million of the `r fmt_m(total_all)` million deaths averted, reflecting the exponential increase in CVD mortality with age (Figure \@ref(fig:fig6-paper)). Adults younger than 70 years accounted for `r fmt_m(averted_lt70)` million averted deaths, representing the prevention of premature CVD mortality --- a metric aligned with SDG target 3.4.

Males accounted for `r fmt_m(averted_male)` million averted deaths and females for `r fmt_m(averted_female)` million, consistent with the higher age-specific CVD mortality rates observed in men. The relative benefit of hypertension control versus lipid-lowering therapy was broadly similar across sex groups, although the absolute number of averted deaths was greater among men for all intervention scenarios (Figure \@ref(fig:fig6-paper)).

## Sensitivity and uncertainty results

The present analysis reports central estimates based on mean input parameters from GBD 2023, meta-analytic effect sizes, and linear scale-up assumptions. Formal probabilistic sensitivity analysis, including propagation of GBD uncertainty intervals and alternative assumptions regarding adherence, secular trends in risk-factor levels, and non-linear scale-up trajectories, is planned as a subsequent extension. The principal findings --- that combined target achievement would avert millions of CVD deaths, that hypertension control contributes the largest single-intervention effect, and that benefits are concentrated in high-burden settings --- are expected to be robust to plausible parameter variation, given the consistent direction and magnitude of evidence from the underlying meta-analyses [@Ettehad2016; @Fulcher2015].

# Discussion

## Principal findings

This study projected that simultaneous achievement of WHO targets for hypertension control and lipid-lowering therapy across `r n_countries` countries from 2026 to 2050 would avert approximately `r fmt_m(total_all)` million CVD deaths and `r fmt_m(total_dalys_all)` million DALYs. Hypertension control in the general population was the single most impactful intervention, averting `r fmt_m(total_bp)` million deaths, while lipid-lowering therapy contributed an additional `r fmt_m(total_stat)` million deaths averted. The multiplicative combination of these interventions yielded substantially greater benefits than any single strategy alone, affirming the complementary nature of blood pressure and lipid management for CVD prevention.

## Interpretation of hypertension control findings

The projected impact of hypertension control is consistent with the well-established dose--response relationship between blood pressure reduction and cardiovascular risk described by Ettehad et al. [-@Ettehad2016], in which every 10 mmHg reduction in systolic blood pressure was associated with a 20% reduction in major cardiovascular events, a 17% reduction in coronary heart disease, and a 27% reduction in stroke (see Hypertension Control Intervention Model for the formal specification). Our findings extend this evidence by quantifying the population-level health gains achievable when these effect sizes are applied at scale across diverse country settings, accounting for heterogeneous baseline blood pressure distributions, varying levels of current hypertension control, and country-specific demographic trajectories.

The concentration of benefits in older age groups reflects the age-dependent increase in both baseline CVD mortality rates and the absolute risk reduction achievable through blood pressure lowering. The consistent benefit across all four modelled CVD causes --- including haemorrhagic stroke and hypertensive heart disease --- underscores the broad pathophysiological relevance of blood pressure control beyond ischaemic outcomes alone.

## Interpretation of lipid-lowering therapy findings

Lipid-lowering therapy with statins was projected to avert `r fmt_m(total_stat)` million deaths, with effects concentrated in ischaemic heart disease and ischaemic stroke. This cause-specific profile is consistent with the atherogenic mechanism of LDL cholesterol and the evidence base from major statin trials, which have demonstrated significant reductions in coronary events and ischaemic stroke with minimal effect on haemorrhagic stroke or hypertensive heart disease [@Fulcher2015] (see Statin Therapy Intervention Model). The modelling of statin effects only in adults aged 40 and above, and only for IHD and ischaemic stroke, represents a conservative approach that may underestimate the total benefit if future evidence supports broader indications or earlier initiation.

Adherence to statin therapy remains a critical implementation challenge. Meta-analytic evidence suggests that real-world statin adherence ranges from 40% to 75% depending on the clinical context and follow-up duration [@Basios2025]. Our model assumed full adherence for newly covered individuals under hypertension therapy and adjusted statin adherence for primary and secondary prevention; true population-level effects may be lower if adherence is suboptimal, particularly in settings with limited health system capacity for long-term medication management.

## Combined policy meaning

The combined scenario demonstrates that hypertension control and lipid-lowering therapy are complementary rather than substitutable interventions. Because blood pressure and LDL cholesterol act through partially independent causal pathways, their multiplicative combination generates health gains greater than the sum of their individual effects (see Multi-State Transition Model). This finding has direct policy relevance: programmes that integrate blood pressure measurement and treatment with lipid assessment and statin therapy --- such as the WHO HEARTS technical package --- can capture these synergistic benefits within existing primary health care platforms [@Banigbe2025; @Moran2024].

The projected `r fmt_m(total_all)` million deaths averted and `r fmt_m(total_dalys_all)` million DALYs averted under the combined scenario represent a substantial return on investment in cardiovascular risk-factor management. Recent costing analyses of the HEARTS programme in low- and middle-income countries have demonstrated favourable cost-effectiveness ratios for integrated hypertension and statin management [@Husain2022HeartsCosting; @Garcia2026HEARTS4Countries], suggesting that the health gains projected here are achievable within realistic resource envelopes.

## Equity and implementation implications

The distribution of projected benefits by income group reveals important equity dimensions. Low-income and lower-middle-income countries, which currently have the lowest levels of hypertension control and statin coverage, stand to gain substantially from global target achievement --- both in absolute numbers and as a proportion of their baseline CVD burden. This finding reinforces the moral and epidemiological case for prioritising cardiovascular risk-factor management in resource-constrained settings, where the return on investment in prevention is highest.

However, realising these gains requires overcoming well-documented implementation barriers, including limited access to essential medicines, insufficient numbers of trained health workers, weak supply chains, and fragmented health information systems. The WHO HEARTS programme has demonstrated that standardised, protocol-based approaches to hypertension management can achieve large-scale coverage expansion in diverse country settings [@Banigbe2025], and similar models are needed for lipid management. National commitment to pharmaceutical procurement, task sharing, and community-based screening and follow-up will be essential to translate these modelled projections into real-world health outcomes.

## Relation to previous literature

Our findings are broadly consistent with, and extend, previous global and regional analyses. Kontis et al. [-@Kontis2019] projected the probability of achieving SDG target 3.4 (a one-third reduction in premature NCD mortality by 2030) and identified inadequate cardiovascular risk-factor control as a major barrier in most countries. The NCD Countdown analyses identified blood pressure management and statin therapy as among the most efficient interventions for reducing premature CVD mortality in low- and middle-income settings [@Watkins2022NCD2030; @Bennett2020NCD2030Path]. Our study complements this work by providing country-specific projections over a 25-year horizon, enabling direct comparison of the relative contribution of each intervention.

The Ford et al. analysis of the decline in US coronary mortality attributed approximately half of the observed reduction to evidence-based treatments, including statins and antihypertensives, and the remainder to risk-factor improvements [@Ford2007]. Similarly, Critchley et al. [-@Critchley2004] demonstrated that unfavourable risk-factor trends could offset treatment gains in rapidly developing countries. Our projections implicitly capture this tension by holding baseline risk-factor levels constant in the BAU scenario: the modelled health gains represent the incremental benefit of treatment scale-up above current trajectories.

## Strengths

This study has several notable strengths. First, it provides comprehensive global coverage across `r n_countries` countries, with country-specific epidemiological and demographic inputs rather than reliance on regional averages. Second, the model explicitly accounts for the interaction between hypertension control and statin therapy through multiplicative effect combination, avoiding the overestimation that would result from additive assumptions. Third, the use of GBD 2023 data and UNWPP 2024 population projections ensures that the analysis reflects the most current global health and demographic evidence. Fourth, the model de-duplicates existing treatment effects by crediting only incremental coverage above baseline, avoiding double-counting of current treatment benefits. Fifth, the 25-year projection horizon captures the long-term compounding of sustained risk-factor reduction, which shorter-horizon models may miss.

## Limitations

Several limitations should be considered when interpreting these results. First, formal probabilistic sensitivity analysis was not conducted; results represent central estimates and do not incorporate uncertainty intervals from GBD inputs, meta-analytic effect sizes, or demographic projections. Second, the model assumes a static blood pressure distribution within countries --- no secular trends in population blood pressure and no endogenous updating as treatment coverage increases --- which may overestimate baseline risk in countries experiencing favourable risk-factor trends. Third, full adherence was assumed for hypertension therapy, and adherence-adjusted estimates for statin therapy may still exceed real-world levels in settings with limited health system capacity. Fourth, the linear scale-up assumption (2026--2030) is a simplification; actual programme expansion may follow non-linear trajectories with initial delays and subsequent acceleration. Fifth, no explicit health-system capacity constraints were modelled, meaning that the scenarios represent technical potential rather than implementation-ready projections. Sixth, COVID-19 excess mortality was modelled only for 2020--2021, and potential long-term cardiovascular sequelae of SARS-CoV-2 infection were not incorporated. Finally, the model does not capture potential interactions between interventions and other concurrent NCD prevention strategies, such as dietary sodium reduction or trans-fat elimination, which may modify the marginal benefit of hypertension control and statin therapy.

# Conclusion

Achievement of WHO targets for hypertension control and lipid-lowering therapy by 2030, sustained through 2050, could avert approximately `r fmt_m(total_all)` million CVD deaths and `r fmt_m(total_dalys_all)` million DALYs across `r n_countries` countries. Hypertension control in the general population and lipid-lowering therapy are complementary strategies whose combined benefit exceeds the sum of their individual effects. The projected health gains are substantial across all world regions and income groups, with the largest proportional benefits accruing to countries with the lowest current treatment coverage. These findings provide a quantitative foundation for accelerated investment in integrated cardiovascular risk-factor management through primary health care, and support the case for sustained political commitment to the WHO NCD targets as a cornerstone of global health policy.

# Tables

**Table 1.** Cumulative CVD deaths averted by intervention scenario, `r study_years`.

```{r table1-paper, echo=FALSE}
tab1 <- copy(dt_cumul)[intervention %in% int_order]
setDT(tab1)
tab1[, intervention := factor(intervention, levels = int_order)]
setorder(tab1, intervention)

tab1_display <- tab1[, .(
  Intervention = intervention,
  `Deaths averted (millions)` = fmt_m(deaths_delayed),
  `Average per year (thousands)` = fmt_k(deaths_delayed / 25),
  `% of BAU deaths` = paste0(round(deaths_delayed / bau_total_deaths * 100, 1), "%")
)]

kable(tab1_display, align = c("l", "r", "r", "r"))
```

*Note: Deaths averted = cumulative difference between business-as-usual and intervention scenario, 2026-2050. All four CVD causes combined: ischaemic heart disease, ischaemic stroke, intracerebral haemorrhage, hypertensive heart disease.*

```{r table2-paper, echo=FALSE}
setDT(dt_cause)
dt_cause[, cause_lbl := fcase(
  cause == "ihd",     "IHD",
  cause == "istroke", "Ischaemic stroke",
  cause == "hstroke", "Haemorrhagic stroke",
  cause == "hhd",     "Hypertensive HD",
  default = cause
)]

dt_t2_wide <- dcast(dt_cause[intervention %in% int_order],
                     intervention ~ cause_lbl,
                     value.var = "deaths_delayed", fill = NA)
dt_t2_wide[, intervention := factor(intervention, levels = int_order)]
setorder(dt_t2_wide, intervention)

cause_cols_display <- setdiff(names(dt_t2_wide), "intervention")
for (col in cause_cols_display) {
  dt_t2_wide[, (col) := fifelse(
    is.na(get(col)), "\u2013",
    fmt_m(get(col), digits = 2)
  )]
}

kable(dt_t2_wide, col.names = c("Intervention", cause_cols_display),
      align = c("l", rep("r", length(cause_cols_display))))
```

*Note: Values in millions. \u2013 = intervention does not affect this cause. Statin effects restricted to IHD and ischaemic stroke.*

### Multi-State Transition Model {#sec:transition-model}

The model comprises three mutually exclusive health states for each cause $c \in \{\text{IHD}, \text{ischaemic stroke}, \text{haemorrhagic stroke}, \text{HHD}\}$:

- **Well** ($W_{a,s,c,t}$): Disease-free individuals at risk of developing cause $c$
- **Sick** ($K_{a,s,c,t}$): Individuals living with prevalent disease $c$
- **Dead** ($D_{a,s,c,t}$): Individuals who have died from cause $c$

Individuals transition between states according to cause-specific incidence rates ($IR$: Well $\to$ Sick), case fatality rates ($CF$: Sick $\to$ Dead), and background mortality ($BG.mx$: exits from Sick; $BG.mx.all$: all-cause mortality applied to the total population). The four causes are modelled jointly but independently within each country--age--sex stratum; population-level accounting is maintained through all-cause mortality applied to the total population.

The model operates in discrete annual time steps with simultaneous age advancement: at each step, individuals at age $a$ in year $t$ advance to age $a+1$ in year $t+1$. New cohorts enter at age 20 each year. The projection period runs from 2017 (calibration start) through 2050.

**State transition equations.** For each location $\ell$, sex $s$, cause $c$, at age $a$ in year $t$, the state occupancies at age $a+1$ in year $t+1$ are:

*New cases:*

$$\text{NewCases}_{a+1,s,c,t+1} = W_{a,s,c,t} \times IR_{a,s,c,t} \times \varepsilon_{IR}(a,s,c,t)$$

*Sick population:*

$$K_{a+1,s,c,t+1} = K_{a,s,c,t} \times \left[1 - CF_{a,s,c,t} \times \varepsilon_{CF}(a,s,c,t) - BG.mx_{a,s,c,t} - covid.mx_{a,s,t}\right] + W_{a,s,c,t} \times IR_{a,s,c,t} \times \varepsilon_{IR}(a,s,c,t)$$

*Disease-specific deaths:*

$$D_{a+1,s,c,t+1} = K_{a,s,c,t} \times CF_{a,s,c,t} \times \varepsilon_{CF}(a,s,c,t)$$

*Total population (updated from external demographic projection):*

$$N_{a+1,s,t+1} = N_{a,s,t} - ALL.mx_{a,s,t}$$

*All-cause mortality:*

$$ALL.mx_{a,s,t} = \sum_c D_{a+1,s,c,t+1} + N_{a+1,s,t+1} \times \left(BG.mx.all_{a,s,t} + covid.mx_{a,s,t}\right)$$

*Well population (computed as residual):*

$$W_{a+1,s,c,t+1} = N_{a+1,s,t+1} - ALL.mx_{a+1,s,t+1} - K_{a+1,s,c,t+1}$$

where $\varepsilon_{IR}$ and $\varepsilon_{CF}$ are the multiplicative effect ratios from the intervention modules (equal to 1 under the business-as-usual scenario). COVID-19 excess mortality ($covid.mx$) is applied only for 2020--2021. All state occupancies are bounded below at zero, and transition rates are capped: $CF \leq 0.99$, $IR \leq 0.99$.

**Initial conditions.** At the model start year (2017) and for each new cohort entering at age 20:

$$K_{20,s,c,t_0} = N_{20,s,c,t_0} \times PREV_{20,s,c}$$

$$D_{20,s,c,t_0} = N_{20,s,c,t_0} \times DIS.mx_{20,s,c}$$

$$W_{20,s,c,t_0} = N_{20,s,c,t_0} \times \left(1 - PREV_{20,s,c} - BG.mx_{20,s,c}\right)$$

**Intervention combination.** When multiple interventions are applied simultaneously, their effect ratios combine multiplicatively:

$$\varepsilon_{IR,\text{total}}(a,s,c,t) = \varepsilon_{IR,\text{BP}}(a,s,c,t) \times \varepsilon_{IR,\text{BP,DM}}(a,s,c,t) \times \varepsilon_{IR,\text{statin}}(a,s,c,t)$$

$$\varepsilon_{CF,\text{total}}(a,s,c,t) = \varepsilon_{CF,\text{BP}}(a,s,c,t) \times \varepsilon_{CF,\text{BP,DM}}(a,s,c,t) \times \varepsilon_{CF,\text{statin}}(a,s,c,t)$$

Each intervention effect ratio defaults to 1 when the intervention is not active, so single-intervention and combined scenarios use the same multiplicative framework.

**Primary outcome.** Cumulative CVD deaths averted over the study period are computed as:

$$\text{Deaths averted} = \sum_{a,s,c,t} D^{\text{BAU}}_{a,s,c,t} - \sum_{a,s,c,t} D^{\text{intervention}}_{a,s,c,t}$$

(Parameter values for all transition rates are listed in the Key Parameter Appendix.)

### Hypertension Control Intervention Model {#sec:htn-model}

The hypertension control intervention modifies incidence and case fatality rates through a multi-step pipeline that integrates blood pressure distributions, GBD relative risks, Ettehad trial effect sizes, and linear coverage scale-up. Only *incremental* coverage above country-specific baseline control is credited with new effects, preventing double-counting of existing treatment benefits.

**Coverage scale-up.** Treatment coverage increases linearly from baseline to target over a specified period. The incremental coverage target above baseline is:

$$\Delta C_{\text{target}} = \max(C_{\text{target}} - C_{\text{baseline}}, 0)$$

The time-varying incremental coverage is:

$$\Delta C(t) = \Delta C_{\text{target}} \times \min\left(\frac{t - T_{\text{start}} + 1}{T_{\text{end}} - T_{\text{start}} + 1},\; 1\right)$$

with boundary conditions: $\Delta C(t) = 0$ for $t < T_{\text{start}}$ and $\Delta C(t) = \Delta C_{\text{target}}$ for $t > T_{\text{end}}$.

Coverage is applied only to hypertensive blood pressure bins ($\geq$ 140 mmHg). For hypertensive bins: $C_0 = C_{\text{baseline}}$ and $C_t(t) = C_{\text{baseline}} + \Delta C(t)$. For non-hypertensive bins ($<$ 140 mmHg): $C_0 = C_t = 0$.

**Step 1: Baseline blood pressure distribution.** The untreated population distribution across eight BP bins ($<$120, 120--129, ..., 180+) is obtained for each age--sex--location stratum: $P(\text{BP}_{\text{cat}} \mid a, s, \ell)$.

**Step 2: Bin-specific baseline incidence via GBD relative risks.** GBD relative risks per 10 mmHg SBP increase above the reference ($<$120 mmHg) are applied as a power function of the distance from reference:

$$RR_{\text{GBD}}(\text{BP}_{\text{cat}}, a, c) = RR_{\text{per10}}^{(\text{SBP}_{\text{mid}} - 120)/10}$$

where $\text{SBP}_{\text{mid}}$ is the midpoint of the BP bin. A normalisation factor anchors bin-level rates to the overall incidence:

$$\alpha_{a,s,c,t} = \sum_{\text{BP}_{\text{cat}}} P(\text{BP}_{\text{cat}}) \times RR_{\text{GBD}}(\text{BP}_{\text{cat}}, a, c)$$

Bin-specific incidence is then:

$$IR_{\text{bin}}(\text{BP}_{\text{cat}}) = \frac{RR_{\text{GBD}}(\text{BP}_{\text{cat}}, a, c) \times IR_{a,s,c,t}}{\alpha_{a,s,c,t}}$$

**Step 3: Diabetes-weighted Ettehad trial effect sizes.** The cumulative BP-reduction effect size for each bin and cause is computed as a diabetes-prevalence-weighted average of Ettehad trial estimates:

$$E_{\text{trial}}(\text{BP}_{\text{cat}}, c) = (1 - w_{\text{DM}}) \times E_{\text{noDM}}(\text{BP}_{\text{cat}}, c) + w_{\text{DM}} \times E_{\text{DM}}(\text{BP}_{\text{cat}}, c)$$

where $w_{\text{DM}}$ is the country-specific diabetes prevalence and $E_{\text{noDM}}$, $E_{\text{DM}}$ are cumulative bin-specific effect sizes from the Ettehad meta-analysis for non-diabetic and diabetic populations respectively.

**Step 4--5: Coverage-adjusted effect sizes.** The trial effect size is adjusted by the incremental coverage above baseline:

$$E_{\text{adj}}(t) = \frac{E_{\text{trial}} \times (C_t(t) - C_0)}{1 - E_{\text{trial}} \times C_0}$$

When $C_0 = 0$ (no prior treatment), this simplifies to $E_{\text{adj}}(t) = E_{\text{trial}} \times C_t(t)$.

**Step 6: New bin-specific incidence.**

$$IR_{\text{bin,new}}(\text{BP}_{\text{cat}}, t) = IR_{\text{bin}}(\text{BP}_{\text{cat}}) \times \left[1 - E_{\text{adj}}(t, \text{BP}_{\text{cat}}, c)\right]$$

**Step 7: Population-weighted aggregate incidence.**

$$IR_{\text{new}}(a, s, c, t) = \sum_{\text{BP}_{\text{cat}}} IR_{\text{bin,new}}(\text{BP}_{\text{cat}}, t) \times P(\text{BP}_{\text{cat}})$$

**Step 8: Incidence effect ratio.**

$$\varepsilon_{IR,\text{BP}}(a, s, c, t) = \frac{IR_{\text{new}}(a, s, c, t)}{IR_{\text{original}}(a, s, c, t)}$$

Values of $\varepsilon_{IR,\text{BP}} < 1$ indicate reductions in disease incidence attributable to the intervention.

**Step 9: Case-fatality effect ratio.** Case fatality reductions are computed from the *incremental* aggregate coverage across hypertensive bins, preventing double-counting of baseline treatment effects:

$$\Delta C_{\text{delta}}(t, \text{BP}_{\text{cat}}) = \max\left(C_t(t) - C_0, 0\right)$$

$$C_{\text{agg}}^{\Delta}(a, s, c, t) = \frac{\sum_{\text{BP}_{\text{cat}} \in \text{HTN}} \Delta C_{\text{delta}}(t, \text{BP}_{\text{cat}}) \times P(\text{BP}_{\text{cat}})}{\sum_{\text{BP}_{\text{cat}} \in \text{HTN}} P(\text{BP}_{\text{cat}})}$$

where the summation is restricted to hypertensive bins (BP $\geq$ 140 mmHg). The case-fatality effect ratio is:

$$\varepsilon_{CF,\text{BP}}(a, s, c, t) = 1 - \rho_{CF,c} \times C_{\text{agg}}^{\Delta}(a, s, c, t)$$

where the cause-specific CF reduction factors are: $\rho_{CF,\text{IHD}} = 0.24$, $\rho_{CF,\text{IS}} = 0.36$, $\rho_{CF,\text{HS}} = 0.76$, $\rho_{CF,\text{HHD}} = 0.20$.

**Step 10.** The final output collapses across BP bins, retaining only the aggregate $IR_{\text{new}}$, $CF_{\text{new}}$, $\varepsilon_{IR,\text{BP}}$, and $\varepsilon_{CF,\text{BP}}$ per age--sex--cause--year stratum.

(See Multi-State Transition Model for the baseline transition structure into which these effect ratios enter; see Key Parameter Appendix for all intervention effect sizes and their sources.)

#### Diabetes Component {#sec:htn-diabetes}

The diabetes-specific hypertension control intervention applies the same pipeline as the general-population intervention with three key modifications:

1. **Coverage target**: $C_{\text{target,DM}} = 0.80$ (versus 0.50 in the general population), corresponding to the Global Diabetes Compact target of 80% blood pressure control among people with diagnosed diabetes.

2. **Diabetes weighting**: The Ettehad effect sizes are computed with $w_{\text{DM}} = 1$ (full diabetes-specific effects), rather than the country-specific diabetes prevalence weight used in the general-population intervention.

3. **Population downscaling**: Because the intervention targets only the diabetic subpopulation, the effect is downscaled by the proportion of the population with diabetes ($d_{a,s,\ell}$) and raised blood pressure ($\phi_{\text{hyp}}$):

*Incidence:*

$$IR_{\text{bin,new}} = IR_{\text{bin}} \times \left(1 - d_{a,s,\ell} \times E_{\text{adj,DM}}(t)\right)$$

*Effect ratio blending (population-level):*

$$\varepsilon_{IR,\text{BP,DM}} = 1 \times (1 - d_{a,s,\ell} \times \phi_{\text{hyp}}) + \varepsilon_{IR,\text{raw}} \times d_{a,s,\ell} \times \phi_{\text{hyp}}$$

This ensures that the diabetes-specific intervention affects only the diabetic hypertensive fraction of the population, with the remainder retaining the baseline (unmodified) transition rate.

*Case fatality* is similarly downscaled: the incremental coverage delta is multiplied by the diabetes prevalence before aggregation, so that CF reductions apply only to the diabetic fraction:

$$\Delta C_{\text{delta,DM}} = d_{a,s,\ell} \times \max(C_t - C_0, 0)$$

The same CF reduction factors ($\rho_{CF,c}$) are applied to this diabetes-adjusted aggregate coverage.

(See Hypertension Control Intervention Model above for the general-population coverage scale-up structure, which shares the same functional form.)

### Statin Therapy Intervention Model {#sec:statin-model}

The statin intervention models the impact of scaling up lipid-lowering therapy among adults, with effects restricted to IHD and ischaemic stroke for ages $\geq 40$ years. The implementation: (i) scales up *incremental* coverage above country-specific baseline (to avoid double-counting), (ii) applies attributable fractions ($AF_{c,\ell}$) only for incidence effects (primary prevention), and (iii) applies trial-based relative risks directly for case fatality effects (secondary prevention), with ischaemic stroke CF effects restricted to the atherosclerotic fraction.

**Eligibility.** Statin effects are applied only to individuals aged $a \geq 40$ and for causes $c \in \{\text{IHD}, \text{ischaemic stroke}\}$. For ages $a < 40$ or other causes, the effect ratios are set to 1 (no effect).

**Coverage scale-up.** The same linear scale-up function is used as for hypertension control (see Hypertension Control Intervention Model). Let $U_{0,\ell}$ denote baseline statin coverage at $T_{\text{stat,start}}$. The incremental target is:

$$\Delta U_{\text{target},\ell} = \max(U_{\text{target}} - U_{0,\ell},\; 0)$$

The time-varying incremental coverage above baseline is:

$$\Delta U(t, \ell) = \Delta U_{\text{target},\ell} \times \min\left(\frac{t - T_{\text{stat,start}} + 1}{T_{\text{stat,end}} - T_{\text{stat,start}} + 1},\; 1\right)$$

with $\Delta U(t,\ell) = 0$ for $t < T_{\text{stat,start}}$ and $\Delta U(t,\ell) = \Delta U_{\text{target},\ell}$ for $t > T_{\text{stat,end}}$.

**Trial-based relative risks and risk reductions.** Per approximately 1 mmol/L LDL-C reduction:

| Cause | $RR^{IR}_c$ | $RR^{CF}_c$ | $\delta^{IR}_c = 1 - RR^{IR}_c$ | $\delta^{CF}_c = 1 - RR^{CF}_c$ |
|-------|------------|------------|------|------|
| IHD | 0.74 | 0.80 | 0.26 | 0.20 |
| Ischaemic stroke | 0.80 | 0.96 | 0.20 | 0.04 |

Table: Statin relative risks from the Cholesterol Treatment Trialists' Collaboration [@Fulcher2015]

**Incidence effect size.** For $c \in \{\text{IHD}, \text{ischaemic stroke}\}$ and $a \geq 40$, the incidence effect size incorporates the cause- and location-specific attributable fraction and a baseline-coverage adjustment in the denominator:

$$E^{IR}_{c,\ell}(t) = \frac{AF_{c,\ell} \times \delta^{IR}_c \times \Delta U(t,\ell) \times \alpha_{IR}}{1 - \delta^{IR}_c \times U_{0,\ell} \times \alpha_{IR}}$$

where $AF_{c,\ell}$ is the attributable fraction from GBD 2021 (default values: $AF_{\text{IHD}} = 0.15$, $AF_{\text{IS}} = 0.12$; country-specific values used where available) and $\alpha_{IR}$ is adherence for primary prevention (default: 1.0).

**Case fatality effect size.** CF effects are modelled directly from trial relative risks without attributable fractions. For ischaemic stroke, only the atherosclerotic fraction contributes:

$$E^{CF}_{c,\ell}(t) = \begin{cases} \dfrac{\delta^{CF}_{\text{IHD}} \times \Delta U(t,\ell) \times \alpha_{CF}}{1 - \delta^{CF}_{\text{IHD}} \times U_{0,\ell} \times \alpha_{CF}} & \text{if } c = \text{IHD} \\[1em] \dfrac{\psi_{\text{athero}} \times \delta^{CF}_{\text{IS}} \times \Delta U(t,\ell) \times \alpha_{CF}}{1 - \delta^{CF}_{\text{IS}} \times U_{0,\ell} \times \alpha_{CF}} & \text{if } c = \text{ischaemic stroke} \end{cases}$$

where $\psi_{\text{athero}} = 0.60$ and $\alpha_{CF}$ is adherence for secondary prevention (default: 1.0).

**Modified rates.** For ages $a \geq 40$ and $c \in \{\text{IHD}, \text{ischaemic stroke}\}$:

$$IR_{\text{new}}(a,s,c,t) = IR(a,s,c,t) \times \left[1 - E^{IR}_{c,\ell}(t)\right]$$

$$CF_{\text{new}}(a,s,c,t) = CF(a,s,c,t) \times \left[1 - E^{CF}_{c,\ell}(t)\right]$$

**Statin effect ratios:**

$$\varepsilon_{IR,\text{statin}}(a,s,c,t) = \begin{cases} 1 - E^{IR}_{c,\ell}(t) & \text{if } a \geq 40 \text{ and } c \in \{\text{IHD}, \text{IS}\} \\ 1 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}$$

$$\varepsilon_{CF,\text{statin}}(a,s,c,t) = \begin{cases} 1 - E^{CF}_{c,\ell}(t) & \text{if } a \geq 40 \text{ and } c \in \{\text{IHD}, \text{IS}\} \\ 1 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}$$

**Combined intervention effect.** When statin and hypertension control interventions are applied simultaneously, their effect ratios combine multiplicatively (see Multi-State Transition Model):

$$\varepsilon_{IR,\text{total}} = \varepsilon_{IR,\text{BP}} \times \varepsilon_{IR,\text{BP,DM}} \times \varepsilon_{IR,\text{statin}}$$

$$\varepsilon_{CF,\text{total}} = \varepsilon_{CF,\text{BP}} \times \varepsilon_{CF,\text{BP,DM}} \times \varepsilon_{CF,\text{statin}}$$

This multiplicative structure means the combined benefit exceeds the sum of individual effects, reflecting the partially independent causal pathways through which blood pressure control and lipid lowering reduce cardiovascular risk.

(See Key Parameter Appendix for all statin effect sizes and their sources.)

### DALY Calculation Methods {#sec:daly-methods}

Burden of disease was quantified using disability-adjusted life years (DALYs), computed as the sum of years of life lost due to premature mortality (YLL) and years lived with disability (YLD). No age weighting or time discounting was applied. All computations were performed separately by age $a$, sex $s$, cause $c$, year $t$, location $\ell$, and intervention scenario $j$.

#### Years of Life Lost (YLL)

YLLs were computed as the product of the number of disease-specific deaths and the remaining life expectancy at the age of death:

$$YLL_{a,s,c,t,\ell,j} = D_{a,s,c,t,\ell,j} \times e_x(a, t, \ell)$$

where $D_{a,s,c,t,\ell,j}$ is the number of CVD deaths from cause $c$ (the `dead` variable from the state-transition model output) and $e_x(a, t, \ell)$ is the remaining life expectancy at exact age $a$ in year $t$ for location $\ell$, taken from the United Nations World Population Prospects 2024 revision, medium variant (both sexes combined). Life expectancy values are country- and year-specific, reflecting projected demographic conditions rather than a fixed global standard.

#### Years Lived with Disability (YLD)

YLDs were computed using a prevalence-based approach as the product of the number of prevalent CVD cases and a cause- and location-specific disability weight:

$$YLD_{a,s,c,t,\ell,j} = K_{a,s,c,t,\ell,j} \times DW_{c,\ell}$$

where $K_{a,s,c,t,\ell,j}$ is the number of individuals in the Sick (prevalent) state for cause $c$ from the state-transition model output, and $DW_{c,\ell}$ is the disability weight for cause $c$ in location $\ell$. Disability weights were derived from GBD 2023 data as the ratio of cause-specific years lived with disability to prevalence for each cause and location:

$$DW_{c,\ell} = \frac{YLD^{\text{GBD}}_{c,\ell}}{Prevalence^{\text{GBD}}_{c,\ell}}$$

This approach yields an implicit, frequency-weighted average disability weight that reflects the severity distribution observed in each country. No explicit duration of disability was modelled; the prevalence-based formulation captures the YLD burden attributable to the stock of prevalent cases at each time point.

#### Disability-Adjusted Life Years (DALY)

Total DALYs were computed as:

$$DALY_{a,s,c,t,\ell,j} = YLL_{a,s,c,t,\ell,j} + YLD_{a,s,c,t,\ell,j}$$

DALYs averted were computed as the difference between the business-as-usual (BAU) scenario and each intervention scenario, summed across all strata:

$$\text{DALYs averted}_j = \sum_{a,s,c,t,\ell} DALY^{\text{BAU}}_{a,s,c,t,\ell} - \sum_{a,s,c,t,\ell} DALY^{j}_{a,s,c,t,\ell}$$

The same differencing logic was applied separately to YLLs averted and YLDs averted.

#### Reference Standards and Weights

```{r daly-param-table, echo=FALSE}
daly_params <- data.frame(
  Parameter = c(
    "Life table standard",
    "Disability weight source",
    "Disability weight derivation",
    "Age weighting",
    "Time discount rate",
    "Duration of disability"
  ),
  Value = c(
    "UNWPP 2024, medium variant",
    "GBD 2023 (IHME)",
    "YLD / Prevalence, by cause and location",
    "None (K = 0)",
    "None --- undiscounted (r = 0)",
    "Prevalence-based (not explicitly modelled)"
  ),
  Year = c(
    "2024",
    "2023",
    "2023",
    "---",
    "---",
    "---"
  ),
  Notes = c(
    "Country- and year-specific remaining life expectancy at exact age x (ex), both sexes combined",
    "IHME-GBD_2023_DATA-52d32656-1",
    "Implicit frequency-weighted severity; country-specific for IHD, ischaemic stroke, haemorrhagic stroke, HHD",
    "Uniform weighting across all ages",
    "Future health losses valued equally regardless of when they occur",
    "YLD = prevalent cases x DW at each annual time step; no explicit incidence x duration calculation"
  ),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)
kable(daly_params, col.names = c("Parameter", "Value or Source", "Year", "Notes"),
      align = c("l", "l", "c", "l"))
```

*Sources: United Nations, Department of Economic and Social Affairs, Population Division (2024). World Population Prospects 2024, Online Edition. Institute for Health Metrics and Evaluation (IHME). Global Burden of Disease Study 2023 (GBD 2023) Results. Seattle, United States: IHME, 2024.*

All DALY, YLL, and YLD results reported in the main manuscript are computed using the above specifications, as implemented in `07_output_dalys.R`.
